'''broad-sighted''' (brâd′sī″ted), ''a.'' Having a wide view. ''Quarterly Rev.''

'''broad-speaking''' (brâd′spē″king), ''a.'' '''1.''' Using vulgar or coarse language; speaking with a vulgar accent.—'''2.''' Speaking plainly out without endeavoring to soften one’s meaning.

'''broad-spoken''' (brâd′spō″kn), ''a.'' Characterized by plainness or coarseness of speech, or by a vulgar accent; unrefined.

'''broad-spread''' (brâd′spred), ''a.'' Widely diffused.

'''broad-spreading''' (brâd′spred″ing), ''a.'' Spreading widely.
{{smaller block|His ''broad-spreading'' leaves.
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. II., iii. 4.}}}}

'''broadstone''' (brâd′stōn), ''n.'' Same as ''ashler.''

'''broadsword''' (brâd′sōrd), ''n.'' A sword with a broad blade, as distinguished from one with a narrow blade or from a three-sided thrusting-sword; a sword of which the edge as well as the point is used. {{smaller|All forms of sword which have a flat blade for cutting are called ''broadswords'', in contrast to swords used for thrusting alone. See ''claymore.''}}

'''broadtail''' (brâd′tāl), ''n.'' One of the numerous

'''broadthroat''' (brâd′thrōt), ''n.'' [< ''broad'' + ''throat''; a translation of ''Eurylæmus'', q. v.] A book-name of birds of the family ''Eurylæmidæ'' (which see). Also called ''broadbill'' and ''broadmouth.''

'''broad-tool''' (brâd′töl), ''n.'' A stone-masons’ chisel with a very wide edge, used for finishing.

'''broad-tread''' (brâd′tred), ''a.'' Having a wide face or tread, as a car-wheel.

'''Broadwell ring.''' See ''ring.''

'''broadwise''' (brâd′wīz), ''adv.'' [< ''broad'' + ''-wise.''] In the direction of the breadth; breadthwise: as, to measure ''broadwise.''

'''broam†''', ''n.'' [Origin obscure; perhaps a misprint.] Apparently, a spirit or goblin.
{{smaller block|The approach of the sun’s radiant beams expelleth goblins, bugbears, hob-thrushes, ''broams'', screech-owl mates, night-walking spirits, and tenebrions.
{{right|''Urquhart'', tr. of Rabelais, iii. 24.}}}}

'''brob''' (brob), ''n.'' [E. dial.; perhaps an alteration of ''brod'', a nail, brad, verb ''brod'', prick: see ''brod''

In ''coal-mining'', a short, thick piece of timber, used for supporting the coal which is being holed or undercut; a prop. [Midland coal-field, England.]

'''brob''' (brob), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''brobbed'', ppr. ''brobbing''. [E. dial., < ''brob'', ''n.''] To prick with a bodkin. ''Halliwell.'' [North. Eng.]

'''Brobdingnagian''' (brob-ding-nag′i-an), ''a.'' and ''n.'' '''I.''' ''a.'' Like or likened to an inhabitant of the fabled region of Brobdingnag in Swift’s “Gulliver’s Travels”; hence, of enormous size; gigantic.
{{smaller block|German prose, as written by the mob of authors, presents, as in a ''Brobdingnagian'' mirror, the most offensive faults of our own.
{{right|''De Quincey'', Style, i.}}}}
'''II.''' ''n.'' A gigantic person.
{{smaller block|“Sally!” screamed the ''Brobdingnagian'', “what bedrooms is disengaged? A gentleman wants a bed.”
{{right|''T. Hook'', Gilbert Gurney, II. v.}}}}

'''broc†''', ''n.'' [F.: see ''bric-à-brac''.] A large vessel with a handle, and generally made of metal or coarse pottery, for holding liquids.

'''brocade''' (brō-kād′), ''n.'' [< Sp. ''brocado'' (= Pg. ''brocado'' = It. ''broccato''; cf. F. ''brocart''), brocade,

{{smaller block|A gala suit of faded ''brocade.''
{{right|''Irving.''}}}}
'''2.''' A kind of bronze-powder used for decorating.

'''brocaded''' (brō-kā′ded), ''a.'' '''1.''' Woven or worked into a brocade.
{{smaller block|''Brocaded'' flowers o’er the gay mantua shine.
{{right|''Gay'', Panthea.}}}}
'''2.''' Dressed in brocade.—'''3.''' Decorated with flowers, etc., in relief: as, a ''brocaded'' silk. [Equivalent to French ''broché.'']

'''brocade-shell''' (brō-kād′shel), ''n.'' A name given to ''Conus geographicus'', one of the cone-shells,

'''brocage''', ''n.'' See ''brokage''.

'''brocard''' (brok′ärd), ''n.'' [< OF. ''brocard'', a maxim (in mod. F. a taunt, jeer, raillery), ML. ''brocardicum'', so called, it is said, from ''Brocard'', prop. ''Burchhard'' or ''Burkard'', bishop of Worms (died 1025), who published a collection of ecclesiastical canons, “Regulæ Ecclesiasticæ,” also known as ''Brocardica'' or ''Brocardicorum opus''.] '''1.''' A law maxim founded on inveterate custom, or borrowed from the Roman law, and accounted part of the common law. Hence—'''2.''' An elementary principle or maxim; a short proverbial rule; a canon.
{{smaller block|The legal ''brocard'', “Falsus in uno, falsus in omnibus,” is a rule not more applicable to other witnesses than to consciousness.
{{right|''Sir W. Hamilton.''}}
The scholastic ''brocard'' [Nihil est in intellectu quod non fuerit in sensu] . . . is the fundamental article in the creed of that school of philosophers who are called “the sensualists.”
{{right|''Ferrier'', Inst. of Metaphysics, p. 261.}}}}

'''brocardic''' (brọ̄-kär′dik), ''n.'' Same as ''brocard''.
{{smaller block|I make use of all the ''brocardics'', or rules of interpreters; that is, not only what is established regularly, in law, but what is concluded wise and reasonable by the best interpreters.
{{right|''Jer. Taylor'', Pref. to Duct. Dub.}}}}

'''brocat†''', ''n.'' An old form of ''brocade''.

'''brocatel, brocatelle''' (brok′a-tel), ''n.'' [< F. ''brocatelle'' = Sp. ''brocatel'', < It. ''broccatello'', variegated marble (F. '''broch''' (broċh), ''n.'' Same as ''brough''<sup>2</sup>.

'''brochan''' (broċh′an), ''n.'' [Gael. Ir. ''brochan'', porridge, gruel.] Oatmeal boiled in water; thick porridge. [Scotland and Ireland.]

'''brochant''' (brō′shant), ''a.'' [F., ppr. of ''brocher'', stitch, etc.: see ''brocade.''] In ''her.'', lying over and covering: said of any bearing which partly covers another. Also ''brouchant.''

'''brochantite''' (brọ̄-shan′tīt), ''n.'' [After ''Brochant'' de Villiers, a French mineralogist (1773–1840).] An emerald-green mineral consisting of hydrous sulphate of copper. The crystals are in thin rectangular and transparent tables.

'''Brochata''' (brọ̄-kā′tä̤), ''n. pl.'' [NL., neut. pl. of ''brochatus'', projecting (of teeth), having projecting teeth (of animals): see ''brochate.''] In Blyth’s classification of mammals, a tribe or suborder of his ''Diplodontia'', corresponding to the ''Pachydermata'', herbivorous ''Cetacea'', and ''Rodentia'' of Cuvier: so called from usually having persistently growing teeth, as the tusks of the elephant or the incisors of a rodent, or projecting tushes, as those of the swine and hippopotamus.
{{smaller block|Blyth divided his ''Brochata'' into ''Proboscidea'', ''Rodentia'', ''Chœrodia'' (swine), and ''Syrenia'' (''Sirenia''), three of which (all excepting ''Chœrodia'') are now recognized orders of ''Mammalia''; but the name is not in use.}}

'''brochate''' (brō′kāt), ''a.'' [< NL. ''brochatus'', having projecting teeth, < L. ''brochus'', ''brocchus'', ''broccus'', projecting (of teeth), having project-
readings.c3s1:
ing teeth (of animals): see ''broach.''] Having tusks, tushes, or perennial teeth; specifically, of or pertaining to the ''Brochata.''

¶
'''broche†''', ''n.'' A Middle English form of ''broach'' and ''brooch''<sup>1</sup>. ''Chaucer.''

'''broché''' (brō-shā′), ''a.'' [F., pp. of ''brocher,'' stitch, sew: see ''broach.''] '''1.''' Sewed or stitched: said of a book which is not bound or covered, except with a paper wrapper. See ''brochure.''—'''2.''' Ornamented in weaving with threads which form a pattern on the surface; brocaded: said of a stuff, specifically of silk: as, a ''broché'' ribbon.

'''brochet''' (brō-shā′), ''n.'' [F., a pike, luce, formerly also a faucet, dim. of ''broche,'' a spit, broach: see ''broach.''] A fish of the family ''Cichlidæ, Crenicichla saxatilis,'' having an elongated form and pointed head, thus slightly resembling a pike. {{smaller|It is highly colored and has an ocellated spot at the root of the tail. It is an inhabitant of the fresh waters of South America and Trinidad. [Local in Trinidad.]}}

'''brochette''' (brō-shet′), ''n.'' [F., dim. of ''broche,'' a spit: see ''broach.''] A skewer to stick meat on, used in cookery.

'''brochure''' (brō-shür′), ''n.'' [F., < ''brocher,'' stitch: see ''broach.''] '''1.''' A pamphlet; an unbound book, of which the sheets are held together by sewing only. See ''broché.''—'''2.''' Specifically, a small pamphlet, or one on a matter of transitory interest.

'''brock<sup>1</sup>''' (brok), ''n.'' [< ME. ''brok,'' < AS. ''broc'' = Dan. ''brok,'' a badger; prob. of Celtic origin: W. ''broch'' = Corn. ''broch'' = Bret. ''broch'' = Gael. Ir. Manx ''broc;'' Ir. also ''brech'' and ''brochd,'' a bad-

ger; prob. so called from its white-streaked face, < W. ''brech'' = Gael. Ir. ''breac'', speckled (see ''brill''); cf. Gael. ''brocach'', ''brucach'', speckled in the face; cf. also Dan. ''broget'', Sw. ''brokig'', party-colored: see ''brocket''. Cf. ''bauson''.] A badger. {{smaller block|Or with pretence of chasing thence the ''brock'',
Send in a cur to worry the whole flock! {{right|''B. Jonson'', Sad Shepherd, i. 2.}}}} {{smaller block|[Sometimes used as a term of reproach. Marry, hang thee, ''brock''! {{right|''Shak.'', T. N., ii. 5.]}}}} '''brock2''' (brok), ''n.'' [Shetland ''bruck'', < ME. *''brok'' (not found), < AS. ''gebroc'', neut., a piece, a fragment (cf. ''broc'', affliction, trouble, fatigue) (= OHG. ''brocco'', MHG. ''brocke'', G. ''brocken'', m., = Dan. ''brokke'' = Goth. ''ga-bruka'', f., a piece; cf. dim. MLG. ''brockel'' = ODan. ''broggel'', a piece, fragment), < ''brecan'' (pp. ''brocen''), break: see ''break'', and cf. ''breach'' with its variants ''breck'', ''brick''1, ''brack''1, etc.; cf. also ''brockle''.] A piece; a fragment. [Prov. Eng. and Scotch.] '''brock2''' (brok), ''v. t.'' [Also ''brok'', = OHG. ''brochōn'', ''brockōn'', MHG. G. ''brocken'' = Dan. ''brokke'', break, crumble; from the noun.] To break, crumble, or cut into bits or shreds. [Scotch.] '''brock3†''', ''v. i.'' [ME. ''brokken'', perhaps a secondary form of ''breken'' (pp. ''broken''), break. Cf. ''brock''2.] To cry out; murmur; complain: a word of somewhat uncertain meaning, found only in the two passages quoted. {{smaller block|What helpth hyt the crokke That hys [is] to felthe [filth] ydo, Aye [against] the crokkere to ''brokke'', “Why madest thou me so?” {{right|''William de Shoreham'', Religious Poems (ed. Wright), p. 106.}}}}

'''brock<sup>4</sup>''' (brok), ''n.'' [E. dial.; cf. ME. ''brok'' (see quot.); cf. Icel. ''brokkr'', also ''brokk-hestr'', a trotter, trotting horse, ''brokka'', trot. Origin and relations uncertain; the alleged AS. “''broc'', an inferior horse, a shaking horse, jade” (Bosworth), does not exist, the def. being due to an error of translation.] A cart-horse or draft-horse: a word of uncertain original meaning, applied also in provincial English to a cow. ''Brockett; Halliwell.''

{{smaller block|<poem>The carter smot and cryde as he were wod,
Hayt ''brok'', hayt scot. {{right|''Chaucer'', Friar’s Tale, l. 245.}}</poem>}}

'''brock<sup>5</sup>''' (brok), ''n.'' [Appar. a var. of ''bruck'', q. v.] The name of an insect. ''Halliwell.'' [Prov. Eng.]

'''brock<sup>6</sup>''' (brok), ''n.'' [Perhaps another use of ''brock''<sup>1</sup>, a badger.] '''1.''' A pig.—'''2.''' Swill for feeding pigs. [North of Ireland.]

'''brock<sup>7</sup>''' (brok), ''n.'' Short for ''brocket''.

'''brock<sup>8</sup>''' (brok), ''n.'' [Possibly shortened from ''broccoli''.] A cabbage. [Prov. Eng.]

'''brock<sup>9</sup>''' (brok), ''n.'' A variant of ''brough''<sup>2</sup>.

'''brockage''' (brok′ạ̄j), ''n.'' [Appar. < ''brock''<sup>2</sup> + ''-age''.] In ''numis.'', an imperfect coin.

{{smaller block|All imperfect coins, curiously termed ''brockages'', are picked out.
{{right|''Ure'', Dict., III. 349.}}}}

{{smaller block|The Vice-Chancellor’s chaire and deske, Proctors, &c. cover’d with ''brocatall'' (a kind of brocade) and cloth of gold.

'''broché''' (brō-shā′), ''a.''   [F., pp. of ''brocher,'' stitch, sew: see ''broach.'']   '''1.''' Sewed or stitched: said of a book which is not bound or covered, except with a paper wrapper. See ''brochure.''—'''2.''' Ornamented in weaving with threads which form a pattern on the surface; brocaded: said of a stuff, specifically of silk: as, a ''broché'' ribbon.

'''brochet''' (brō-shā′), ''n.''   [F., a pike, luce, formerly also a faucet, dim. of ''broche,'' a spit, broach: see ''broach.'']   A fish of the family ''Cichlidæ, Crenicichla saxatilis,'' having an elongated form and pointed head, thus slightly resembling a pike. {{smaller|It is highly colored and has an ocellated spot at the root of the tail. It is an inhabitant of the fresh waters of South America and Trinidad. [Local in Trinidad.]}}

'''brochette''' (brō-shet′), ''n.''   [F., dim. of ''broche,'' a spit: see ''broach.'']   A skewer to stick meat on, used in cookery.

'''brochure''' (brō-shür′), ''n.''   [F., < ''brocher,'' stitch: see ''broach.'']   '''1.''' A pamphlet; an unbound book, of which the sheets are held together by sewing only. See ''broché.''—'''2.''' Specifically, a small pamphlet, or one on a matter of transitory interest.

'''brock<sup>1</sup>''' (brok), ''n.''   [< ME. ''brok,'' < AS. ''broc'' = Dan. ''brok,'' a badger; prob. of Celtic origin: W. ''broch'' = Corn. ''broch'' = Bret. ''broch'' = Gael. Ir. Manx ''broc;'' Ir. also ''brech'' and ''brochd,'' a badger; prob. so called from its white-streaked face, < W. ''brech'' = Gael. Ir. ''breac'', speckled (see ''brill''); cf. Gael. ''brocach'', ''brucach'', speckled in the face; cf. also Dan. ''broget'', Sw. ''brokig'', party-colored: see ''brocket''. Cf. ''bauson''.]   A badger.
{{smaller block|<poem>Or with pretence of chasing thence the ''brock'',
Send in a cur to worry the whole flock!</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Sad Shepherd, i. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|[Sometimes used as a term of reproach.
Marry, hang thee, ''brock''! {{right|''Shak.'', T. N., ii. 5.]}}}}

'''brock<sup>2</sup>''' (brok), ''n.''   [Shetland ''bruck'', < ME. *''brok'' (not found), < AS. ''gebroc'', neut., a piece, a fragment (cf. ''broc'', affliction, trouble, fatigue) (= OHG. ''brocco'', MHG. ''brocke'', G. ''brocken'', m., = Dan. ''brokke'' = Goth. ''ga-bruka'', f., a piece; cf. dim. MLG. ''brockel'' = ODan. ''broggel'', a piece, fragment), < ''brecan'' (pp. ''brocen''), break: see ''break'', and cf. ''breach'' with its variants ''breck'', ''brick''<sup>1</sup>, ''brack''<sup>1</sup>, etc.; cf. also ''brockle''.]   A piece; a fragment. [Prov. Eng. and Scotch.]

'''brock<sup>2</sup>''' (brok), ''v. t.''   [Also ''brok'', = OHG. ''brochōn'', ''brockōn'', MHG. G. ''brocken'' = Dan. ''brokke'', break, crumble; from the noun.]   To break, crumble, or cut into bits or shreds. [Scotch.]

'''brock<sup>3</sup>†''', ''v. i.''   [ME. ''brokken'', perhaps a secondary form of ''breken'' (pp. ''broken''), break. Cf. ''brock''<sup>2</sup>.]   To cry out; murmur; complain: a word of somewhat uncertain meaning, found only in the two passages quoted.
{{smaller block|<poem>What helpth hyt the crokke
That hys [is] to felthe [filth] ydo,
Aye [against] the crokkere to ''brokke'',
“Why madest thou me so?”</poem>
{{right|''William de Shoreham'', Religious Poems (ed. Wright), p. 106.}}}}
{{smaller block|He singeth ''brokkynge'' [var. ''crowyng'', Wright, Morris] as a nyghtingale.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Miller’s Tale, l. 191.}}}}

'''brock<sup>4</sup>''' (brok), ''n.''   [E. dial.; cf. ME. ''brok'' (see quot.); cf. Icel. ''brokkr'', also ''brokk-hestr'', a trotter, trotting horse, ''brokka'', trot. Origin and relations uncertain; the alleged AS. “''broc'', an inferior horse, a shaking horse, jade” (Bosworth), does not exist, the def. being due to an error of translation.]   A cart-horse or draft-horse: a word of uncertain original meaning, applied also in provincial English to a cow.   ''Brockett; Halliwell.''

<poem>The carter smot and cryde as he were wod,
Hayt ''brok'', hayt scot. {{right|''Chaucer'', Friar’s Tale, l. 245.}}</poem>

'''brock<sup>5</sup>''' (brok), ''n.''   [Appar. a var. of ''bruck'', q. v.]   The name of an insect.   ''Halliwell.'' [Prov. Eng.]

'''brock<sup>6</sup>''' (brok), ''n.''   [Perhaps another use of ''brock''<sup>1</sup>, a badger.]   '''1.''' A pig.—'''2.''' Swill for feeding pigs. [North of Ireland.]

'''brock<sup>7</sup>''' (brok), ''n.'' Short for ''brocket''.

'''brock<sup>8</sup>''' (brok), ''n.''   [Possibly shortened from ''broccoli''.]   A cabbage. [Prov. Eng.]

'''brock<sup>9</sup>''' (brok), ''n.'' A variant of ''brough''<sup>2</sup>.

'''brockage''' (brok′ạ̄j), ''n.''   [Appar. < ''brock''<sup>2</sup> + ''-age''.]   In ''numis.'', an imperfect coin.

{{smaller block|All imperfect coins, curiously termed ''brockages'', are picked out.
{{right|''Ure'', Dict., III. 349.}}}}

'''brocket''' (brok′et), ''a.''   [< Dan. ''broget'', older form *''broket'', party-colored: see ''brock''<sup>1</sup>.]   Va-<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
